title: Cowen & Keltner (2017), Self-report captures 27 distinct categories of emotion bridged by continuous gradients
scope: Conceptual anchor for fuzzy emotional categories and a small set of explicitly identified semantic neighbors.
limitations: Video-elicited reports from a particular study are not a universal inventory or temporal transition probabilities. HEA editorial entries are not a reproduction of its category map.

title: Nummenmaa et al. (2014), Bodily maps of emotions
scope: Anchor for discussing emotion together with subjective bodily experience.
limitations: Self-reported sensations do not establish diagnostic bodily fingerprints; HEA illustrations are not measurements from this study.

title: Tangney, Stuewig & Mashek (2007), Moral emotions and moral behavior
scope: Conceptual distinctions among shame, guilt, embarrassment, pride, and related self-evaluation.
limitations: Review-level support for distinctions; not proof of every HEA example or proposed transition. Cultural and theoretical alternatives remain.

title: Larsen, McGraw & Cacioppo (2001), Can people feel happy and sad at the same time?
scope: Evidence that happiness and sadness can coexist; conceptual starting point for explicitly editorial mixtures.
limitations: Does not validate every combination or establish a universal mixture formula. Other HEA mixtures are editorial constructions.

title: Larsen et al. (2021), Meaningful endings and mixed emotions: The double-edged sword of reminiscence on good times
scope: Meaningful endings, reminiscence, and mixed feelings.
limitations: Study contexts do not cover all nostalgia, grief, or cultures; no fixed emotional sequence follows.

title: Parrott & Smith (1993), Distinguishing the experiences of envy and jealousy
scope: Comparison of envy and jealousy using recollection and experimentally manipulated stories.
limitations: Conceptual distinctions and reported associations do not prove what any individual feels or whether a relationship threat is real.

title: Lange, Weidman & Crusius (2018), The painful duality of envy
scope: Distinguishes forms of envy and their relationship with schadenfreude.
limitations: The association depends on how envy is defined; envy does not inevitably become pleasure at misfortune.

title: Palmer et al. (2024), Sleep loss and emotion: A systematic review and meta-analysis of over 50 years of experimental research
scope: Sleep reduction can influence emotional functioning; supports including bodily context.
limitations: Group-level experimental effects are not a diagnosis or a cause attribution for an individual. Overwhelm descriptions are editorial extensions, not a named finding.

title: Emmons & McCullough (2003), Counting blessings versus burdens
scope: Gratitude and subjective well-being in structured diary studies.
limitations: Does not imply that gratitude must be induced or that it reliably removes another emotion.

title: Buddhagupta, An Extensive Commentary on the Four Immeasurables, translated at Lotsawa House
scope: Conceptual source for goodwill, compassion, appreciative joy, and equanimity.
limitations: Tradition-specific contemplative account; not population statistics. HEA offers short original descriptions, not the translation or its full doctrinal meanings.

title: AN 5.161, Removing Annoyance, translated by Ñanamoli Thera
scope: Traditional association of annoyance with cultivation of goodwill, compassion, and equanimity.
limitations: Describes practice in a monastic teaching context, not a guaranteed interpersonal remedy. Linked translation retains its own rights; it is not republished in HEA.

title: Shantideva, Engaging in Bodhisattva Behavior, chapter 6, translated by Alexander Berzin
scope: Traditional contrast between anger and cultivated patience.
limitations: Ethical and contemplative teaching, not empirical proof that patience changes a particular emotional episode. No translation passages are reproduced.

title: SN 36.6, The Arrow, translated by Thanissaro Bhikkhu
scope: Distinction between painful feeling and additional mental reactivity.
limitations: Feeling tone in this discourse is not identical to the modern category emotion. Acceptance links are editorial comparisons, not an exact translation.

title: Clinical Care Considerations for Bereaved Patients (2022)
scope: Varied experiences during bereavement, including sorrow, numbness, and anger.
limitations: Bereavement context does not explain every instance of emotional numbness; HEA does not diagnose or prescribe care.

title: Schriber et al. (2017), Dispositional Contempt: A First Look at the Contemptuous Person
scope: Contempt and distinctions from neighboring interpersonal emotions.
limitations: Much evidence concerns dispositions rather than individual episodes; cannot be used to infer personality from one utterance.

title: The state of boredom: Frustrating or depressing? (2018)
scope: Relationship between boredom, frustration, and task autonomy.
limitations: Findings are conditional on studied tasks; boredom and frustration are neither equivalent nor an inevitable sequence.

title: Arnold, Kappes, Klinenberg & Winkielman (2021), The Role of Comparisons in Judgments of Loneliness
scope: Direct conceptual anchor for loneliness as perceived insufficiency of social connection. Experiments, survey data, and interviews examine social and temporal comparisons.
limitations: Studies concern selected United States and British samples and comparison tasks. They do not establish a universal intensity scale, duration, bodily cue, or individual response to contact. HEA transition examples remain editorial.

title: Leknes et al. (2011), Relief as a reward: hedonic and neural responses to safety from pain
scope: Direct evidence for pleasant relief when expected pain is avoided, and for the relevance of negative expectations.
limitations: A small healthy-volunteer laboratory pain study. Generalization to social, financial, or bereavement contexts is editorial; brain measures do not identify an individual’s emotion from language.

title: Franklin, Lee, Hanna & Prinstein (2013), Feeling worse to feel better: pain-offset relief simultaneously stimulates positive affect and reduces negative affect
scope: Laboratory evidence concerning relief after pain ends, distinguishing positive affect from reduction of negative affect.
limitations: Pain-offset results do not establish that all forms of relief are calm, have a fixed duration, or replace all other feelings. Everyday examples and relationships in HEA are editorial extensions.

title: Martínez, van Prooijen & Van Lange (2022), Hate: Toward understanding its distinctive features across interpersonal and intergroup targets
scope: Compares reported hate with dislike, anger, contempt, and disgust, including perceived threat, arousal, and action tendencies toward interpersonal and intergroup targets.
limitations: United States adult self-reports about targets; group comparisons do not establish a universal definition or prove an individual’s intent. Reported attack-oriented tendencies are not equivalent to enacted violence. Object-directed hatred in HEA remains an editorial extension.
